summary: At just 9.2 square miles, National City packs nearly 59,000 residents into one of the densest footprints in the San Diego metro — over 6,400 people per square mile — yet it sits directly on San Diego Bay, meaning some blocks open onto waterfront views that would cost double in neighboring Coronado or downtown San Diego. The city is genuinely flat, a low-lying coastal plain wedged between the bay to the west and Interstate 805 to the east, with the massive National City Marine Terminal and naval facilities anchoring the western edge — a reminder that military logistics and port operations are major local economic engines alongside healthcare jobs at nearby hospitals. That infrastructure gives the city a working, industrial-port texture rather than a polished waterfront-resort feel, and the freeway corridors do fragment the grid, creating pockets that don't always connect smoothly on foot. Affordability tells a complicated story: the median home sits at roughly $581,000 against a median household income of about $64,200, yielding a price-to-income ratio above 9:1 — steep even by Southern California standards — while median rent at $1,619 consumes roughly 30% of that same income. Year-round highs averaging 71°F with over nine hours of daily sunshine make the mild climate one of the genuine, unambiguous perks. National City is a place where bay-adjacent geography and port-city grit coexist in a permanent, uneasy tension with Southern California housing math.
